articles.title: inDrive Eyes 2027 Robotaxi Tests With Pony.ai and NVIDIA
articles.description: Ride-hailing platform inDrive has joined hands with Pony.ai and NVIDIA to explore bringing robotaxis to the country, with Astana identified as the first proposed market. The companies announced on October 23 that they had signed a memorandum of understanding (MOU) to assess the feasibility of autonomous ride-hailing. The collaboration will examine whether Level 4-ready vehicles can operate through inDrive's existing platform while meeting local safety, regulatory and commercial requirements. The announcement comes as autonomous driving companies look beyond their established markets. For inDrive, which operates across more than 1,200 cities in 47 countries, the collaboration offers an opportunity to understand how driverless vehicles could fit into its mobility business. However, the companies are still evaluating the project. A commercial launch will depend on an agreement with the government of Kazakhstan. Why Kazakhstan? Kazakhstan has been developing a regulatory framework for driverless transportation as part of its broader focus on digitalization and artificial intelligence. According to inDrive, the country has introduced its first structured legal framework for autonomous transport, creating an opportunity to explore how the technology could work on public roads. Astana, the country's capital, has been selected for the proposed initial launch. With a population of around 1.7 million and growing transportation needs, the city offers a potential market for autonomous ride-hailing. But Astana also presents a challenge that makes the project particularly interesting. The city experiences long, harsh winters, with snow and icy roads that can make driving difficult. For autonomous vehicles, these conditions raise important questions about navigation, vehicle control and reliable operation. Arsen Tomsky, Founder and CEO of inDrive, said the project could provide useful insights into how autonomous vehicles perform in such environments. "Launching here will provide an important opportunity to evaluate autonomous driving technology in challenging winter conditions." The company believes the experience could help it assess similar services in other locations that face demanding weather conditions. How the Technology Will Work The collaboration brings together three companies with different responsibilities. Pony.ai will provide its seventh-generation robotaxis, while inDrive will make the service available through its ride-hailing application and manage operations. NVIDIA will support the initiative with AI infrastructure, including NVIDIA Hyperion, a reference sensor and computing platform designed for Level 4 autonomous vehicles. The major NVIDIA robotaxi technology platform also combines the Alpamayo software stack and NVIDIA Halos safety system. Pony.ai's Gen-7 robotaxis incorporate multiple sensors, system-level redundancy and fail-operational capabilities intended to support reliable autonomous operations. The company has already deployed its autonomous driving technology in commercial operations in major Chinese cities and expanded its presence across several international markets. However, adapting that technology to Kazakhstan will require the partners to examine local road conditions, operational requirements and regulatory compliance. The announcement does not specify the number of vehicles planned for the proposed launch or the exact configuration of the technology to be deployed. Moving Into New Markets For inDrive, the proposed project offers a way to explore autonomous mobility within an existing ride-hailing network. Rather than announcing a new standalone robotaxi service, the companies intend to evaluate how autonomous vehicles could be offered to passengers through the inDrive app. That could help determine whether driverless transportation can complement conventional ride-hailing services. The partnership also reflects a broader shift in autonomous mobility, where driving technology developers, AI infrastructure providers and consumer platforms bring together their capabilities to explore commercial deployment. For Pony.ai, Kazakhstan represents another opportunity to assess its technology outside China. For NVIDIA, the collaboration provides a potential application for its autonomous driving infrastructure in a new operating environment. Still, integrating these technologies into a working ride-hailing service will require more than technical readiness. The partners must also assess how the service would operate, comply with local regulations and remain commercially viable. What Still Needs to Be Decided? Although the companies have outlined their responsibilities, several details remain open. The announcement does not provide a launch date, fleet size, ride pricing or projected investment. It also does not explain how the proposed service would manage daily operations or what conditions would need to be met before passengers could book autonomous rides. These questions matter because developing a self-driving vehicle and operating a reliable commercial service are different challenges. The companies will need to evaluate how the vehicles perform on local roads, how they integrate with inDrive's platform and whether the operating model makes financial sense. If the initial launch in Astana moves forward, inDrive and Pony.ai plan to assess whether the approach could be extended to other cities in Kazakhstan and additional markets where inDrive operates. For now, the agreement represents an early step toward exploring autonomous ride-hailing rather than a confirmed rollout. The real significance of the collaboration lies in what it could reveal about bringing driverless transportation to new markets, particularly those with demanding road conditions. For inDrive, Pony.ai and NVIDIA, Kazakhstan could become an important test of whether autonomous driving technology is ready to move beyond existing deployments and become part of everyday urban transportation.

articles.title: THUD: NPR Host A Martinez Gets an 'F' on Trump's Popularity In Israel
articles.description: THUD: NPR Host A Martinez Gets an 'F' on Trump's Popularity In Israel Screenshot from Patrick Strattner photo for NPR On Thursday's Morning Edition, NPR anchor A Martinez (not the soap-opera actor) interviewed Rand Corporation expert Shira Efron, who was in Tel Aviv, on the closeness of President Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Efron talked up how it could be like joint election interference: "If you remember, during Trump's first term, and Netanyahu was prime minister, Netanyahu basically received, if you will, the policy choices by the United States that supported his government the whole time. And Netanyahu himself has basically intervened in U.S. elections - endorsing Trump, visiting him in Mar-a-Lago in the summer of 2024 in the middle of election campaigns." But as Netanyahu runs for re-election the NPR anchor naturally assumed -- wrongly -- that Trump was a big drag on Bibi's ticket: "You mentioned how Netanyahu is lagging in the polls. How much is his relationship with President Trump part of the reason? Or all of it, maybe?" Efron had to tell him he was dead wrong: EFRON: Well, actually, President Trump still enjoys very high approval ratings in Israel. If I remember the numbers correctly, even after some Israeli disappointment from the interim outcome in Iran in the summer, his approval ratings among the Jewish population moved from the 90s to close to 80%. So it would have - actually supposed to boost Netanyahu's credentials. Many Israelis - and this is something that I think would - is important to know for outsiders - even those who are very much in the opposition and would do anything in their power to remove Netanyahu from government - they still have tremendous respect for Trump because they think that the Israeli hostages would not have returned home if it wasn't for the interference of the - and the pressure of the president. Martinez (actual first name: George) just closed out the interview, and skulked out of the embarrassment. articles.title: South Africa: Durban mayoral candidate says he would welcome Netanyahu despite ICC warrant
articles.description: South Africa: Durban mayoral candidate says he would welcome Netanyahu despite ICC warrant Submitted by Azad Essa on Fri, 10/23/2026 - 21:09 Democratic Alliance mayoral candidate Haniff Hoosen says he would welcome the Israeli prime minister to Durban if it benefited residents Haniff Hoosen is the Democratic Alliance's eThekwini mayoral candidate (DA KZN) Off A South African mayoral candidate running in the coastal city of Durban has drawn outrage and ridicule after saying he would welcome Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu if the visit would benefit the city. Haniff Hoosen, the Democratic Alliance’s candidate for eThekwini mayor, made the remarks during a mayoral debate earlier this week, according to a video circulated by local media. Asked whether he would receive Netanyahu, should he travel to the city, the 54-year-old Hoosen answered: "Why shouldn't I if he comes to visit the city?" "If there is a benefit for the people of the city through that visit, I will certainly do it," he added. Haniff said Durban was "falling apart" and that, as mayor, his primary focus would be improving conditions for people living in the city. Netanyahu is wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC), which issued an arrest warrant against him in November 2024 over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip. More than 250,000 Palestinians have been killed or injured in the genocide in Gaza. As a party to the Rome Statute, South Africa is obligated to cooperate with the ICC. Attacks on Navi Pillay Haniff's comments come two weeks after Duban-born Navi Pillay was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for her lifelong efforts to uphold international law. Pillay recently chaired the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory in 2025, which declared that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Observers have noted that while the South African government publicly congratulated Pillay for the honour, the Democratic Alliance - the party to which Haniff belongs - has yet to issue a statement. Meanwhile, the Nobel Prize ushered in fierce backlash from the South African Zionist Federation as well as other pro-Israel advocates in the country. One South African commentator who now lives in Israel described the award as "a stain on the rule of international law and justice". When pressed by journalists after the debate, Hoosen stood by his position. He said he spoke “the truth” all the time and that “people will know what they can expect from me”. “What I will not do is tell people one thing and do something completely different,” he said. Hoosen's willingness to welcome Netanyahu contrasts with South Africa’s pursuit of accountability for Israel at the International Court of Justice (ICJ). His remarks come ahead of South Africa’s local government elections on 4 November. Several political parties are vying for control of eThekwini amid widespread frustration over water shortages, sewage spills, crime, and deteriorating infrastructure. This has culminated in rising incidents of crime and deadly attacks on Black African foreigners. Earlier this week, police said that a mob of close to 50 people killed a Black African migrant in the Durban city centre.
